meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never was anything great achieved without danger'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited everywhere to Machiavelli, yet found in none of his works and never sourced. Here's what he actually wrote about danger and greatness.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Machiavelli on virtually every quotation site, and the sentiment squares with his writing on the peril of bold action — yet the sentence appears in none of his works (The Prince, the Discourses on Livy, the Art of War or the Life of Castruccio Castracani) and no source ever names one. It is best read as a modern distillation of his ideas rather than a line he actually wrote.

source.excerpt: Never was anything great achieved without danger.
trail: Every major quote site — Goodreads ↗, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes — credits Machiavelli but names no book or chapter, and Goodreads itself flags that its quotes are “not verified.”
The sentence is absent from The Prince ↗ and does not appear in Machiavelli’s sourced Wikiquote entry ↗.
Its nearest authentic root is the Discourses on Livy ↗ (Bk I, ch. 2): a state “can never be reformed without great risk.”
source.excerptNote: No manuscript or printed work of Machiavelli’s is known to contain this sentence. The nearest authentic parallel is in the Discourses on Livy (Bk I, ch. 2), where he warns that a state “can never be reformed without great risk,” because the necessity for change “cannot arise without danger” (Gutenberg full text ↗).
source.rightsNote: Machiavelli’s own writings have been in the public domain for centuries. This particular English sentence, however, cannot be traced to any of them; treat it as an anonymous modern paraphrase of his outlook rather than a quotation with a rights-holder.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: About Niccolò Machiavelli
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political theorist whose treatise The Prince (written 1513) made his name a byword for hard-edged statecraft. His major works — The Prince, the Discourses on Livy, the Art of War and the Florentine Histories — return repeatedly to the theme that founding or reforming a state is dangerous, risky work. That reputation makes him a magnet for punchy “risk and greatness” aphorisms, many of which he never actually wrote.

cite.sourceCitation: Widely attributed to Niccolò Machiavelli in modern quotation collections (e.g., Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZQuotes); no primary source in his works has been identified. Nearest authentic parallel: Niccolò Machiavelli, Discourses on the First Decade of Titus Livius, Bk I, ch. 2.

misattribution.heading: How it’s mis-cited
misattribution.intro: The line is presented almost everywhere as a verbatim Machiavelli quotation — frequently pinned to The Prince — but it is really a case of confident mis-citation: a real Machiavellian mood attached to words he did not write.

items.scope: Frequently cited as a line from
items.why: The phrase occurs nowhere in The Prince. The book’s nearest thought is that there is nothing “more perilous to conduct … than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things” (ch. 6, Gutenberg ↗) — a related idea in entirely different words.

Bk I, ch. 2 says a state “can never be reformed without great risk” and that the necessity for change “cannot arise without danger” (Gutenberg ↗). That is the genuine kernel the aphorism distills — but it is not this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: No known work by Machiavelli, and no edition of his quotations on Wikiquote ↗, contains ‘Never was anything great achieved without danger.’ It is best regarded as an unsourced distillation of his outlook, not something he actually wrote.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Machiavelli
lead: The attribution endures because it is plausible. Machiavelli built his whole political vision around the idea that great acts — founding a state, reforming a corrupt republic, seizing and holding power — are inseparable from risk. A reader who meets “Never was anything great achieved without danger” and is told it is Machiavelli feels no friction, because it sounds exactly like him.

That plausibility is also what lets an unsourced line travel unchecked. Quote aggregators copy one another, none of them cites a chapter, and the sentence acquires the authority of repetition rather than of a page in any of his books.
context.pull: It sounds like Machiavelli — which is precisely why no one checks whether he wrote it.
